content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper constructed a procedure-generated spatial reasoning task to test impact of name on LLM, in this case BLOOM, a LLM trained with multiple languages. In the experiments, it shows that while the largest BLOOM performs fairly well on the task, the performance is impacted significantly by the language and gender. Notably, the performance gap increases when changing the language as the model size increases. Additionally, it found the model is poorly calibrated and self-explanation can be used for error detection.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- It studies the impact of names on LLM spatial reasoning capability and document failure cases of LLM.

Weakness:
- It’s unclear how popular names are defined.
- One could interpret the result as BLOOM does not learn equally high quality LM for all the supported languages instead of bias on certain names. Note that the training dataset is inherently imbalanced. It would strengthen the study if there’s a controlled group that don’t contains real names, i.e. generic names like A/B/C, male/female 1/2/3 etc.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is well written although some experiment details are missing, making it non-trivial to reproduce. The research question is novel. However, the experiment could be improved.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the research question and finding are interesting, the experimental design is limited. As a result, I’m leaning towards reject.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies the spatial reasoning problem with the BLOOM language model and investigates the bias due to name choices in the examples. The task formulation is that the input is a paragraph about the spatial relations between person names. And the question is about who is on the left of a given person mentioned above.

They found that the BLOOM model is not well-calibrated and thus it is hard to detect reasoning errors. Therefore, they propose to create two follow-up questions for BLOOM to justify its answers by themselves. This is a self-explanation method for inspecting the error and bias of models. With this, they found the bias (i.e., the variation) in different countries in terms of the name changes, can be pretty different --- almost 0 in US and 0.3 in China.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength

- An interesting finding that can improve the robustness of spatial reasoning in terms of name changes in non-US countries. 

- A self-reflect method for spatial reasoning in BLOOM LMs that can detect errors better. 



## Weakness

- The study of the paper is overly specific and may only be attractive to a minimal number of the ICLR community. The task is a simple toy task of spatial reasoning with synthetic data. The model is only the BLOOM model. The number of studied countries is also limited. 

- There is no detailed analysis of why such name bias will happen. 

- There is no solution to improve such name-based robustness in spatial reasoning. 

- The self-reflect method to better detect bias and errors of LMs is interesting but it is only limited to the toy spatial reasoning task in this paper now. 

Please see more suggestions and questions in the Summary section.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The presentation of the paper is mostly okay. The novelty is very limited, though. I would suggest authors remove the algorithms or move them into the appendix as they are not that helpful.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I think the paper may be very interesting to some NLP workshops but not ready for ICLR. Overall, the paper is more like an empirical analysis of a very specific question that is not generally interesting to the audience. 

I hope the authors can expand their study to a broader context if they want to improve the paper:

- Expand the scope of tasks. I don't see how spatial reasoning is so special or particularly important for studying LLMs. The other real NLP tasks may also have such robustness issues with name bias (e.g., reading comprehension[1], NER[2], relation extraction, etc.). 

- Study the reasons behind such bias and errors. Why BLOOM has this scenario? And is it also the case for other LLMs like OPT, GPT-J, and T0? They are all open and free, so I don't see why BLOOM is the only LMs for us to study.

- Generalize the follow-up questions to other tasks so you can make the self-explanation a more general technique.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes an automated synthesis and an error analysis of a spatial reasoning task over the names of people (proper names) for BLOOM models. 

**The paper’s contributions are the following:**
-  **Definition and creation of a spatial reasoning task over people's names:** The goal is to analyze their bias with respect to the used proper names. The authors do so by creating a method to automatically generate data samples for this task and then zero-shot the BLOOM models to test their performance.

-  **Analysis of BLOOM limitations on this task:** The authors study personal names as a new source of variations in the performance of large language models even when the underlying reasoning task ought to be independent of the choice of the former. They test BLOOM models by changing the number of individuals over which spatial reasoning needs to be performed. They conclude that there exists 1) a spatial bias between countries, and 2) a gender bias between female and male proper names.

-  **Error detection using model self-explanations:** They suggest a new way to assess model uncertainty by calibrating model probabilities through self-explanation prompts. They perform error detection by prompting the model to generate a textual explanation that reflects the model’s internal view of its reasoning. 

This paper's overall findings suggest that BLOOM models are substantially influenced by the choice of personal names on this task.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Major strengths:**
- Identifying the biases in proper names between countries and genders is a highly important mission for both efficiency and ethical purposes in the NLP and language model domain.
- The authors provide a detailed analysis of the spatial reasoning tasks for proper names by stressing the BLOOM models on various numbers of individuals and assessing their reasoning efficacy.
- The use of prompting mechanisms is a very promising technique to pick inside models' reasoning capabilities. 
- Ethical biases in ML and AI should be addressed by model creators and this paper provides an interesting approach to evaluate a model’s reasoning.


**Weaknesses:**
- **Prompting mechanism:** While the idea of prompting a model to understand its implicit reasoning using self-explanations of its predictions is a promising direction, the implementation should take into account the multi-factor nature of the problem. More specifically, the results presented in this paper are heavily influenced and biased by the choice of the prompt and the way the pre-training of the tested models has been implemented. In order to have concrete conclusions about the reasoning mechanics of a model, both the pre-training data distributions as well as a variety of used prompts should be considered. In other words, what are the distributions of proper names in the dataset that the model was pre-trained on? And how this acts as a co-founding factor to the presented results? The authors partially acknowledge these questions, however, fail to answer them.

- **Accuracy variations due to the country of the personal names:** Authors test the capability of BLOOM models to predict the correct proper name in the spatial reasoning task by selecting a number of names for each country. They later claim that they exist biases among countries and that variation from proper names needs to be addressed to avoid biased analyses. However, cross-country analysis should also be made (i.e. names from different countries in the same example) in order to reach the claim of spatial bias.

-  **Error detection using model self-explanations:** Authors propose a new approach using the model’s self-explanation for error detection. The provided results are referring to the self-explanation performance compared to the golden labels. However, no analysis of how this approach is compared with the one with no self-explanation is mentioned. Additionally, no strong pieces of evidence are provided regarding the intersection of the wrong predictions made both by the zero-shot approach as well as the proposed one (with self-explanations).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The written and presentation quality and clarity of this paper meet expectations. The methodology and experiments were very detailed and presented with both textual and visual aids.

The originality of this work was limited to the use of existing methodologies (task creation, models, and prompts for self-explanation).
content.summary_of_the_review:
While the idea and motivation behind the problem of proper name usage and their bias in state-of-the-art LMs are pragmatic, I believe that the authors should put more work into identifying the co-founding factors in order to back up their results and motivation with more substantial pieces of evidence. 

Further experiments (additional and diverse prompts) and analysis (understanding and presenting the co-founding factors alongside experiments) should be made in order to make this work innovative and valuable to the language model research community.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper creates a synthetic zero-shot task for large language models (LLMs), each instance is defining an order of people using left/right relations, e.g. "John is on the right of David. James is on the left of David. James is on the left of John. Joseph is on the right of James. John is on the left of Joseph. Then, we can make a new inference that David is on the left of", where the model is expected to fill in an appropriate name.

They evaluate BLOOM models of various sizes on datasets with either 3 or 4 individuals in the setup. 

For the 4-individual task they find accuracies from about 30% to 80% as model size increases from 0.5B to 176B, if the names are all common American male names. If names are pulled from a different region, e.g, India or China, a drop of up to 20% in accuracy is found. Such a variance indicates a problematic hidden issue in the models.

They find that the modes are poorly calibrated on this task, as the log probability associated with the generated answer token is only very weakly correlated with correctness.

They find that continuing the answer generation with a further zero-shot explanation prompt ("... inference that David is on the left of Joseph because the list of names from left to right is") will elicit a list of names, and in a 1-shot fashion they can ask the model whether the list if compatible with their statement. The accuracy of this second order ("System 2") verification is found to be around 60-80% across different name origins.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
  - Examplifies the types of hidden (and unexpected?) biases and sensitivies that can exist in LLMs


Weaknesses:
  - The task seems rather unrelated to proper names, one could easily have substituted other objects like variables (X, Y, Z), nouns (car, house, bike), garbled words (sdff, qtwx, griq), etc. They mention that the effect could be due to term-frequency in training data. Another effect could be number of subword tokens in the objects. These should be relatively simple to check independent of the country dependency, which might then turn out to be more of a red herring

  - The "System 2" verification shares similarities with work on (zero shot) "chain of thought" prompting, but with just post hoc verification (no chance for the model to recover), so no simple way to measure improvements in overall accuracy.

  - A few-shot version of the prompting might be worthwhile to check as well
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written and straightforward to follow. The connection between the synthetic task and which proper names are used seems too artificial, and more basic reasons for the variations should be checked.

The "System 2" prompting has been covered in more generality in other work and the version here is not easy to make practical use of. So although this has seeds of interesting ideas, at this point it is not particularly novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: The narrow scope of the task, and the artificial connection to proper name bias, makes it hard to recommend this work. There are seeds of interesting findings and novel prompting techniques, but for the most part they are subsumed by concurrent work which is much broader.

content.title: What's in a name? The Influence of Personal Names on Spatial Reasoning in BLOOM Large Language Models
content.abstract: Large language models have been shown to exhibit reasoning capability. But the ability of these models to truly comprehend the reasoning task is not yet clear. An ideal model capable of reasoning would not be affected by the names of the entities over which the relations are defined. In this paper, we consider an algorithmically generated spatial reasoning task over the names of persons. We show that the choice of names has a significant impact on the reasoning accuracy of BLOOM large language models. Using popular names from different countries of the world, we show that BLOOM large language models are susceptible to undesirable variations in reasoning ability even though the underlying logical reasoning challenge does not depend on these names. We further identify that the conditional log probability scores characterizing the uncertainty in prediction produced by BLOOM models are not well-calibrated and cannot be used to detect such reasoning errors. We then suggest a new approach based on model self-explanations and iterative model introspection that performs better than BLOOM conditional log probability scores in detecting such errors and may help alleviate the bias exhibited by these models.
